A.explanation: With $v_s = 110\text{ m s}^{-1}$ the observed frequency is $1000 \times 330/(330-110) = 1500\text{ Hz}$, matching the measurement.

B.explanation: This is half the speed of sound and would give $f_o = 1000 \times 330/165 = 2000\text{ Hz}$, larger than the observed $1500\text{ Hz}$.

C.explanation: This value makes $330 - v_s = 110\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and predicts $f_o = 3000\text{ Hz}$, because the wavelength is shortened too much.

D.explanation: A source speed equal to the speed of sound would give zero observed wavelength and a very large frequency, not $1500\text{ Hz}$.

hints: Notice the source of $1000\text{ Hz}$ directly approaches the stationary observer, so successive wavefronts are crowded together and the observer hears $1500\text{ Hz}$ with a shorter wavelength.
For an approaching source use $f_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$ where $v = 330\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is the speed of sound and $v_s$ is the unknown source speed.
Set $1500 = 1000 \times 330/(330 - v_s)$ and solve for $330 - v_s$ first, then find $v_s$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: List the useful data: source frequency $f_s = 1000\text{ Hz}$, observed frequency $f_o = 1500\text{ Hz}$, wave speed $v = 330\text{ m s}^{-1}$, source speed $v_s$ unknown with source moving toward stationary observer.
State the Doppler rule for this case: the observed wavelength is shortened to $\lambda_o = (v - v_s)/f_s$, so the observed frequency is $f_o = v/\lambda_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$.
Rearrange for the denominator: $v - v_s = v \times (f_s/f_o)$.
Substitute values with units: $v - v_s = 330\text{ m s}^{-1} \times (1000/1500) = 330\text{ m s}^{-1} \times (2/3) = 220\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Solve for the source speed: $v_s = 330\text{ m s}^{-1} - 220\text{ m s}^{-1} = 110\text{ m s}^{-1}$, with a unit check that all terms are speeds.
